how-to-split-shared-kitchen-costs-fairly.text:
← back to the calculator

How to split shared kitchen costs fairly

Fairly, in a commissary with tenants who use the space unevenly, does not mean dividing the pooled bill by the number of tenants. On one real $5,000 pool, an even split overcharges the lightest tenant by 84% and undercharges the heaviest by 35% — the same pool, the same tenants, just a different arithmetic.

The same $5,000 pool, three different splits

This calculator's own verified defaults: a $5,000 monthly pool (rent, utilities, trash, cleaning, pest control, insurance) across three tenants booking 40, 25, and 15 hours, with a $75 flat base fee each.

TenantHours bookedEven splitHours-only splitBlended split (default)
Truck 140$1,666.66$2,462.50$2,564.82
Truck 225$1,666.67$1,567.19$1,528.82
Truck 315$1,666.67$970.31$906.36

All three columns sum to exactly $5,000.00. Only the method of dividing it changes.

The light tenant pays the most, proportionally, under an even split

Truck 3 books 15 of the pool's 80 total tenant-hours — about 19% of the usage — but an even split would charge it a flat third of the bill, $1,666.67. The default blended split charges it $906.36 instead: an even split overcharges this tenant by about 84%. Nobody decided to overcharge the light user on purpose; it is just what dividing by headcount does when usage is not actually even.

The heavy tenant is the one being subsidized

Truck 1 books half the pool's total tenant-hours and carries the most storage, and the blended split charges it $2,564.82 for that. An even split would only charge it $1,666.66 — about 35% less. The $898.16 difference does not disappear; it is paid by Trucks 2 and 3, who use the kitchen less but split the shortfall evenly anyway.

Hours and storage are not interchangeable

An hours-only split ($2,462.50 / $1,567.19 / $970.31) lands close to the blended one on these defaults, but not identical — because storage tracks a different cost than booked hours. A tenant who rents a full walk-in shelf but rarely cooks on-site would pay almost nothing under an hours-only split; the blended method (70% hours, 30% storage by default, adjustable) prevents that gap.

Common questions

How do you split shared kitchen costs fairly?

By usage, not by headcount: split the pooled monthly cost (rent, utilities, trash, cleaning, pest control, insurance) by hours booked, storage units used, or a blend of both, instead of dividing it evenly across every tenant. This calculator's own verified defaults — a $5,000 pool across three tenants booking 40, 25, and 15 hours — price a 70/30 hours/storage blend at $2,564.82, $1,528.82, and $906.36. Splitting the same pool evenly would charge all three $1,666.67 or $1,666.66.

How much does an even split overcharge the lightest tenant?

On this calculator's defaults, the lightest tenant (15 hours booked, one dry storage unit) owes $906.36 under the default blended split but $1,666.67 under an even split — about 84% more, for a tenant using roughly a third of the kitchen's booked hours.

How much does an even split undercharge the heaviest tenant?

On this calculator's defaults, the heaviest tenant (40 hours booked, the most storage) owes $2,564.82 under the default blended split but only $1,666.66 under an even split — about 35% less, meaning the lighter tenants are covering the gap every month without anyone deciding that on purpose.

Why split by both hours and storage instead of just hours?

Because they track different costs. Booked hours track variable costs like utilities and staff oversight; storage units track a more fixed draw on the walk-in and freezer space regardless of how many hours a tenant actually cooks on-site. On this calculator's defaults, an hours-only split prices the same three tenants at $2,462.50, $1,567.19, and $970.31 — close to the blended figures, but not identical, because a storage-heavy, hours-light tenant is not the same as an hours-heavy, storage-light one.

FOR COMMISSARY & SHARED-KITCHEN OPERATORS

Split the kitchen bill by who actually uses it.

A shared commissary bills one pooled rent, utility, trash, cleaning, and pest-control total every month, but the tenants booking it don't use it evenly. This free calculator splits that pool by hours booked and storage used instead of splitting it evenly or arguing about it, and gives you a clean itemized bill for each tenant.

Pooled monthly costs

List each shared cost. Blank rows are ignored, and the amounts sum automatically.

Cost itemAmount ($)

Leave this blank to use the sum of the itemized costs above. Fill it in only if you'd rather type one total.

Split method

Only used for the weighted blend method above. 70% hours / 30% storage is a starting point, not a rule — set it to whatever mix reflects your own kitchen's costs.

Tenants

List each tenant with their hours booked and storage units used this period. Blank rows (no name) are ignored. Base fee is optional and charged before the proportional split.

Billing outlook

Total billed always equals the pool total to the cent — nothing is left over and nothing is double-counted, whatever split method you choose.

Per-tenant breakdown

Copies every tenant's base fee, proportional share, and total, plus the pool total and split method, as plain text to paste into an email or invoice.

Private by default

Everything on this page runs in your browser and nothing is ever uploaded. There is no account and no server-side storage of any kind — your costs, tenant names, hours, storage counts, and fees are never saved or sent anywhere, and refreshing the page clears them by design. We count only anonymous local feature events (split_calculated, breakdown_copied, reset, sponsor_link_clicked) so we can tell whether the calculator gets used — no costs, tenant names, or amounts are recorded, and Do Not Track / Global Privacy Control turn it off automatically.

Common questions

How should a commissary kitchen split costs among food trucks?

By usage, not headcount. A tenant who books 40 hours a week and fills a walk-in shelf is using far more of the pooled rent, utilities, and cleaning than one who stops in for 5 hours to prep. Splitting by hours booked and storage units used charges each tenant roughly what their footprint actually costs; an even split charges the light user for the heavy user's share every month.

What if one tenant barely uses the kitchen?

Under an hours- or storage-based split, a tenant with very little booked time and no storage owes very little of the proportional pool — their bill is close to just the flat base fee, if one is charged. That is the point of splitting by usage instead of by tenant count: a light user's bill should look light.

Is an equal split ever fair?

When usage is genuinely similar — a handful of trucks each booking roughly the same hours and storage — an equal split is fair and simpler to explain, and the equal-split option here exists for exactly that case. It stops being fair the moment one tenant's usage diverges meaningfully from the rest, which is the case a usage-based split is for.

Why do the default blend weights favor hours over storage?

70% hours / 30% storage is a starting point, not a rule, chosen because booked kitchen time is usually the larger driver of a commissary's variable cost (utilities, cleaning, staff oversight) while storage is a smaller, more fixed draw. Every kitchen's cost mix is different — the two weights are inputs you can set to whatever split reflects your own costs.

Does anything about my tenants or costs get uploaded?

No. Every number on this page runs in your browser only. Nothing is sent to a server, there is no account, and nothing about your costs, tenants, hours, or storage is ever saved or uploaded. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button below.

Also pricing a single food-truck event or catering booking, not a recurring shared kitchen bill? The food truck event margin calculator finds the real price for one booking after commissary prep, travel, staff, and turnout risk — a different job than splitting this kitchen's monthly bill.

See this calculator vs. splitting the kitchen bill evenly for what a usage-based split catches that dividing by tenant count doesn't, or how to split shared kitchen costs fairly for the worked numbers.

← back to the calculator

This calculator vs. splitting the kitchen bill evenly

Dividing a commissary kitchen's pooled monthly costs by the number of tenants is the simplest possible split, and it needs no calculator at all. The problem is that "simple" and "fair" are only the same thing when every tenant uses the kitchen about the same amount — and in a shared commissary, they usually don't.

Where an even split usually goes wrong

SituationEven splitWhat this calculator does
A tenant books far more hours than the othersPays the same share as everyone else, regardless of how much of the kitchen's time they actually occupy.Splits by hours booked (or blends it with storage), so a heavier user's share reflects the hours they actually used.
A tenant rents a full walk-in shelf but rarely cooks on-siteAn hours-only intuition undercharges them; an even split overcharges the light-hours tenants to compensate for nothing in particular.The storage-based or blended method counts dry, refrigerated, and freezer units separately, so a storage-heavy tenant's share reflects that.
A tenant with almost no usage this periodStill pays a full equal share.Their proportional share is close to zero — they owe close to just their flat base fee, if one is charged.
Rounding the split to whole centsA hand or spreadsheet split that rounds each tenant's share independently can leave a few cents of the pool unaccounted for.A largest-remainder allocation guarantees every tenant total sums exactly to the pool total, to the cent.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

What's wrong with just splitting the pooled cost evenly across every tenant?

Nothing, if every tenant genuinely uses the kitchen about the same amount. It goes wrong the moment usage diverges: a tenant who books 40 hours a week and fills a walk-in shelf pays the same as one who stops in for 5 hours to prep, and the light user is quietly subsidizing the heavy one every month.

Why split by both hours and storage instead of just hours?

Because the two drive different costs. Booked hours track variable costs like utilities and staff oversight; storage units track a more fixed draw on the walk-in and freezer space regardless of how many hours a tenant is actually cooking. A tenant who rents a full walk-in shelf but rarely cooks on-site would pay almost nothing under an hours-only split, which is why the blended method exists.

How does this avoid the rounding errors a spreadsheet split usually has?

Every dollar figure is tracked in integer cents internally, and the proportional shares are allocated with a largest-remainder method: each tenant's ideal share is rounded to the nearest cent, then any leftover or shortfall cent is assigned to the tenants whose rounded share moved furthest from their ideal one. A plain spreadsheet formula that rounds each share independently can leave a few cents of the pool unaccounted for; this calculator's tenant totals always sum exactly to the pool total.

Does this replace a written shared-kitchen or tenant agreement?

No. This calculator only does the arithmetic on the costs, hours, and storage figures you enter. It does not draft, review, or enforce any agreement between the commissary operator and its tenants — that stays a conversation and a contract between the people involved.
